title: Tenant circuit breaker explain and replay instructions
content:
Summary

On 2029-05-14 between ~09:42 UTC and ~10:18 UTC we triggered an automated tenant-scoped circuit-breaker (CBF) for streaming text-generation requests that caused mid-stream session truncation for a subset of customers using streaming APIs. The CBF was protective: it prevented an escalating set of stuck inference sessions from depleting shared serving hosts and causing a larger cross-tenant outage, but it did result in partial response truncation for affected streaming sessions and approximately 0.8% higher 5xx rates for streaming endpoints in the window.

Scope and impact

- Impacted surface: Streaming generation (POST /v1/streams and SDK streaming clients) for models in the hosted cluster pool in us-west-2.
- Percentage of customers affected: ~0.6% of active tenants during the window experienced at least one truncated/early-terminated streaming response.
- Behavioral impact: Some streaming sessions returned an early end-of-stream marker or silence in the middle of a generation. Non-streaming (non-HTTP-stream) requests were not materially affected.
- Duration: The initial burst and active CBF period was ~36 minutes (09:42–10:18 UTC); remediation work extended minor follow-ups until 12:00 UTC for system stabilization.

What happened (concise technical explanation)

- Root cause (short): A combination of unusually long-running KV-cache warmups for a small set of tenant model versions and a new conservative circuit-breaker heuristic caused session-level circuit trips that closed streaming sessions without a graceful retry. A recent change in CBF tuning (rolled 2029-05-10) tightened the threshold for session stall detection; this produced false positives under a short-lived traffic mix with long-context prefix loads.
- How the circuit-breaker works (high level): CBF is tenant-scoped and monitors per-session progress (tokens emitted per second, KV-load latencies). If a session appears stalled per threshold rules, the CBF will cut the session to protect host resources. It is designed to fail fast for bad sessions and keep capacity available for the rest of the tenant and cross-tenant pool.

Immediate mitigation we applied

1) Tuned the CBF thresholds to restore expected streaming tolerance for known long-context patterns (rolled 09:58 UTC). This reduced the recurrence rate for the triggering pattern by ~98%.
2) Deployed a streaming-session grace handler that, for sessions cut by CBF, attempts a single transparent retry on a different host when the request is idempotent and the client has requested restart semantics (rolled 10:12 UTC).
3) Rebalanced affected model-serving hosts to flush the KV-cache warmup backlog and evict stuck sessions (completed 11:10 UTC).
4) Issued temporary routing rules to give priority to active streaming sessions from tenants with high SLA requirements while we validated fixes (10:20–12:00 UTC).

Current status (as of last_modified)

- All automated fixes are deployed to us-west-2 and CBF thresholds are reverted to the prior baseline for affected host classes.
- The streaming-session grace handler is enabled for idempotent requests by default in the region.
- We continue to monitor for residual oscillation; no ongoing customer-impacting events detected in the last 72 hours.

Customer actions and recommended mitigations

We recommend the following steps for customers who saw truncated streaming sessions or who rely on uninterrupted streaming:

1) Client-side: enable resume/retry semantics for streaming:
   - If your SDK integration uses streaming, add a lightweight retry path that can re-open a stream on 5xx or an early termination marker and append or deduplicate tokens on your side. Our SDKs (v2.4.1+) include helpers for this (see linked artifact).
2) Request tenant replay evidence bundle:
   - If you need us to validate whether specific user sessions were truncated, request a replay-evidence bundle (see how to request below). The bundle contains token-log traces, host assignment, timestamps per chunk, and a replay script to reproduce the session on our side.
3) Configuration: if you operate long-context warmups or custom prefix caching, add an explicit per-request header X-Redwood-Stream-Hint: long-prefix to opt into our longer warmup allowance (backwards compatible, applied only in private/enterprise and hosted with opt-in).

How to request a replay-evidence bundle

- What we need from you: tenant-id, list of affected request ids (if available), approximate user-visible timestamps (UTC), and a short description of the scenario.
- Where to file: open a support ticket with severity 'incident-evidence' or email cs@redwood.ai. We will provide a secure artifact (S3 link) with the bundle within 48 hours for production customers and within 5 business days for self-serve customers.

Compensation and credits

- For customers who can demonstrate material business impact (for example, revenue loss or end-user harm) tied to truncated streaming responses during the window, we will prioritize a case review and provide account credits up to one billing cycle equivalent for verified impact. Initiate via your account rep or the support ticket and include the replay-evidence bundle request.

FAQ and clarifications

Q: Will this happen again?
A: We pushed an immediate revert for the overly-aggressive threshold and are adding a canary phase for future CBF tuning changes with traffic-simulated validation. We also added a per-tenant historical-profile check to reduce false positives for long-context warmups. While any automated defense can have edge cases, we expect the frequency of false-positive session cuts to be negligible after the changes.

Q: Why not just remove the circuit-breaker?
A: The circuit-breaker is a safety mechanism that prevents a single runaway pattern from starving hosts and causing a cross-tenant outage. Removing it would increase the blast radius for stuck sessions. The goal is to improve tolerance and observability rather than remove protection.

Q: How will you prevent data loss during cut sessions?
A: Streaming responses are best-effort; we strongly recommend application-level resume/deduplication. For customers using session persistence via our tokens API, we provide helpers to reconcile partial results. Replay bundles allow us to reproduce the server-side behavior for any given session.

What we will do next (follow-ups)

- Complete a full postmortem (internal) with timeline, RCA, and preventive actions by 2029-05-28. A customer-facing postmortem (redacted for PII and internal hosts) will be published to the Status page and shared with impacted tenants by 2029-05-30.
- Implement a canary gating step for CBF threshold changes that runs against a replay-simulated long-context workload.
- Add a short telemetry flag in SDKs to automatically surface long-prefix patterns to our observability pipeline (opt-in) to reduce future false positives.

Contact and escalation

- Primary CS contact: Asha Patel (asha@redwood.ai) — include ticket id or tenant id in the subject.
- Engineering liaison for technical reproductions: Marco Liu (marco@redwood.ai).
- For enterprise customers with an account rep: please escalate via your rep for prioritized handling and credits.

Appendix: quick timeline (selected events)

- 09:42 UTC — First alert: increased session stall metric for us-west-2 streaming hosts.
- 09:48 UTC — Automated CBF triggers for multiple tenant sessions; customer-impacting early terminations observed.
- 09:58 UTC — Emergency rollback of the newest strict threshold and partial threshold tuning applied.
- 10:12 UTC — Streaming-session grace handler rolled for idempotent retries.
- 10:20 UTC — Temporary routing priority rules applied for high-SLA tenants.
- 11:10 UTC — Host rebalance completed; KV-cache backlog cleared.
- 12:00 UTC — Major mitigation work completed; monitoring mode entered.

Notes to internal readers

- Please keep this draft internal until the postmortem review is published. If you are tagged on the support ticket or Confluence draft, coordinate language with CS and eng-incident-response to avoid conflicting guidance.

End of brief.
